biblionetwork: edges of bibliometric networks

Source: R/biblionetwork-package.R
biblionetwork-package.Rd

Bibliometric networks are built from tables of links between two kinds of items: documents and the references they cite, authors and the documents they sign. biblionetwork turns such a table into the edges of a one-mode network, whose nodes are one of the two kinds of items, with several ways of weighting the ties. It returns plain tables (data.table), ready to be turned into a graph with tidygraph or igraph, and is the first step of the networkflow pipeline, which projects, clusters and draws the networks.

Which function for which question?

NodesTieFunction
citing documentsshare references (Kessler 1963)biblio_coupling(), by default the cosine of coupling_angle() (Sen and Gan 1983)
citing documentsshare rare referencescoupling_strength(), coupling_similarity() (Shen et al. 2019)
citing documentsother classic normalisationscoupling_jaccard() (Sen and Gan 1983) , coupling_vladutz() (Vladutz and Cook 1984)
citing documentscite different but related references (similar titles)coupling_descriptive() (Liu 2017)
cited referencesare cited together (Small 1973)biblio_cocitation()
authors, institutions, countriesco-sign documentscoauth_network()
entities (authors, journals...)their documents cite the same references, or are cited togetherentity_network(): not a new measure, the aggregation of the measures above at the level of entities

The measures of coupling do not give the same weights: compute_couplings() computes several of them at once, and summarise_weights(), correlate_weights(), overlap_top_weights() and plot_weights() compare the distributions and the rankings of their weights.

Coupling ties are fixed when documents are published, so they suit the comparison of successive time windows; co-citation ties depend on later citations and describe the reception of the cited documents. The vignette vignette("Using_biblionetwork") illustrates all the functions on the data of the package (the literature explaining the US stagflation of the 1970s, (Goutsmedt 2021) ).

Conventions shared by all the functions

  • the input is a table of links with the names of two columns; it is never modified;

  • networks are undirected: each pair of nodes appears once, in the columns Source and Target; from and to are copies, because tidygraph modifies them;

  • duplicated rows are counted once; rows with missing identifiers are dropped with a warning;

  • if no pair of nodes is linked, a warning explains why (nothing shared, or a weight_threshold that is too high) and a table with zero rows and the usual columns is returned;

  • all the measures are computed from the whole table: the weights depend on the corpus.

References

Goutsmedt A (2021). “From the Stagflation to the Great Inflation: Explaining the US Economy of the 1970s.” Revue d'Economie Politique, Forthcoming. https://aurelien-goutsmedt.com/media/pdf/stagflation-great-inflation.pdf.

Kessler MM (1963). “Bibliographic Coupling between Scientific Papers.” American Documentation, 14(1), 10–25. doi:10.1002/asi.5090140103 .

Liu R (2017). “A New Bibliographic Coupling Measure with Descriptive Capability.” Scientometrics, 110(2), 915–935. doi:10.1007/s11192-016-2196-7 .

Sen SK, Gan SK (1983). “A Mathematical Extension of the Idea of Bibliographic Coupling and Its Applications.” Annals of library science and documentation, 30(2).

Shen S, Zhu D, Rousseau R, Su X, Wang D (2019). “A Refined Method for Computing Bibliographic Coupling Strengths.” Journal of Informetrics, 13(2), 605–615. https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1751157716300244.

Small H (1973). “Co-Citation in the Scientific Literature: A New Measure of the Relationship between Two Documents.” Journal of the American Society for Information Science, 24(4), 265–269. doi:10.1002/asi.4630240406 .

Vladutz G, Cook J (1984). “Bibliographic Coupling and Subject Relatedness.” Proceedings of the American Society for Information Science, 21, 204–207.
